items.item: Enum discriminant validity and &raw const/&raw mut are named and explained in post-notes rather than measured directly, since measuring the first would require constructing an invalid enum (the exact UB this chapter's own rule forbids) and the second is a syntactic tool for avoiding an intermediate reference rather than its own separate rule to check.

Stacked Borrows and Tree Borrows are named in post-notes as the formal aliasing model Miri checks against, rather than hand-simulated here, since safely modeling either one in a few lines of ordinary Rust would not genuinely represent what the real model checks; topic 79 covers directly what a checker built on a model like this can and cannot catch.

static mut references being denied by default in Rust 2024 is explained in post-notes as a lint promoted to deny-by-default, not a new validity or provenance rule, and is connected directly to the aliasing violation Stacked Borrows and Tree Borrows exist to catch.

The specific byte values, candidate addresses, and array length used throughout this topic's own scenarios are this specific example's own choice; the measured claims illustrate the real shape of a validity check and a real provenance round trip for any type with these properties, not a claim bound to exactly these numbers.
